title: The water you drink, the fire you light
hookLine: have you seen the water you drink, the fire you kindle, who made them (56:68–72)
tomorrow: None touch it but the purified

lines: NOBODY STANDS AT THE SINK AMAZED.
cards: Turn on a tap and water comes out. Click a lighter and there's a flame. Both happen so often they don't feel like events.

Nobody stands at the sink amazed. Surah Al-Waqi'ah, after its great pictures of the Day, turns to the kitchen. It asks four short questions about four ordinary things: the seed of life, the crop, the water, the fire.
Each starts the same way: have you seen? Have you really looked?

teach.h: HAVE YOU SEEN THE WATER YOU DRINK?
teach.b: Verse sixty-eight. Pickthall: "Have ye observed the water which ye drink?" Then the question behind it: is it you who bring it down from the rain cloud, or are We the ones who send it?
And a sharp line: if God willed, he could make it bitter, salt; so why don't you give thanks?
The same pattern comes a few verses earlier, with the seed from which a person is made, and with the crop: you plant, but who makes it grow? Then the fire. Have you seen the fire you strike?
Was it you who made its tree grow, or did God?
The Arabs of the time struck fire from green wood. Commentators name two desert trees, markh and 'afar, whose branches were rubbed together to make a flame.
Surah Ya-Sin says it too: God made fire for you out of the green tree.
Verse seventy-three gives fire two jobs: a reminder, and a comfort for travelers in the desert, who needed it to cook, to keep warm, to be seen at night. These aren't trick questions.
Nobody listening thought they made the rain. The point is the habit of asking. Every glass of water arrives from somewhere: a cloud, a river, a pipe someone laid.
A hadith turns drinking into a small, slow act.
Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ would breathe three times while drinking, three sips rather than one gulp. Three pauses, enough to notice what's in your hand.

how: Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after, and follow the Prophet's practice of drinking in sips with pauses for breath; these verses of Al-Waqi'ah are recited as a reminder to be grateful for ordinary things.

o: have you seen? have you really looked?
give thanks, said over food and drink
in the name of God, said before eating

games.q: four questions in Al-Waqi'ah — tap the pairs.
p: who sends it from the cloud?

s: the verse says the water could have been made bitter
if God willed, it could be salt and bitter; so why not give thanks?
the surah asks these questions to trick people into a wrong answer
nobody thought they made the rain; the point is the habit of asking.
the Qur'an says fire comes from the green tree
Al-Waqi'ah and Ya-Sin both point to fire struck from green wood.

games.q: you've just poured a glass of water. how does the hadith in Muslim describe the Prophet drinking?
o: in one long drink, without stopping.
games.why: he would breathe three times while drinking, taking it in sips with pauses.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or picture one, and if you can, light a candle safely and watch the flame for a few breaths. Then drink slowly, in three sips, letting today's question rise with each: who made it?
If you pray, you can begin with bismillah and end with alhamdulillah.

wordCard.voice: Afara'aytum: have you seen? The question Surah Al-Waqi'ah asks four times, of the water, the seed, the crop and the fire. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: have you seen the water that you drink? afara'aytum, have you seen, opens each of the four questions.

carryVoice: Your line: who made it? Every glass of water arrives from somewhere. That's day six hundred ten.
